title: Mathematical Background: Robertson's Derivation
content: The docstring outlines the Robertson 1929 derivation of the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. For Hermitian operators A and B acting on a Hilbert space, taking f = (A − ⟨A⟩)ψ and g = (B − ⟨B⟩)ψ converts standard deviations σ_A = ‖f‖ and σ_B = ‖g‖ into norms. The commutator expectation ⟨[A,B]⟩ = ⟨ψ|AB − BA|ψ⟩ then equals 2i·Im⟨f,g⟩, so extracting the imaginary part from Cauchy-Schwarz directly yields the variance bound.

title: Cauchy-Schwarz: The Foundational Inequality
content: This theorem wraps Mathlib's `inner_mul_le_norm_mul_sq` in the complex setting. The result states that the squared modulus of the inner product is bounded by the product of squared norms. The proof is a one-liner: Mathlib's lemma applies directly to any `InnerProductSpace ℂ E`. This establishes the first step of the Robertson chain.

title: Imaginary Part Bound: Dropping the Real Part
content: The key algebraic step: for any complex number z = a + bi, we have b² ≤ a² + b² = |z|². This is proved by `linarith` from `sq_nonneg z.re`. This bound is what converts the full modulus inequality from Cauchy-Schwarz into a one-sided constraint on the imaginary part alone — exactly the part that captures the commutator ⟨[A,B]⟩.

title: Robertson Core: The Abstract Uncertainty Kernel
content: This is the reusable heart of all Robertson-type uncertainty relations. By chaining im_sq_le_normSq with cauchy_schwarz_sq via a `calc` block, we obtain (Im⟨f,g⟩)² ≤ ‖f‖²·‖g‖² for any f, g in any complex inner product space. When f = (A−⟨A⟩)ψ and g = (B−⟨B⟩)ψ, this directly gives σ_A²·σ_B² ≥ (Im⟨f,g⟩)² = |⟨[A,B]⟩|²/4.

title: Heisenberg Bound: Substituting the Commutator
content: The physical content enters here: assuming Im⟨f,g⟩ = c/2 (which holds when f = ΔX·ψ, g = ΔP·ψ, and [X,P] = iℏ with c = ℏ), we rewrite using `hc` and derive c²/4 ≤ ‖f‖²·‖g‖² by `linarith`. The substitution is purely syntactic — no physics is hardcoded, making the theorem applicable to any pair of operators satisfying the canonical commutation relation.

title: uncertainty_principle: Named Physical Instance
content: This theorem gives the physically meaningful statement: for positive ℏ and the commutator hypothesis Im⟨f,g⟩ = ℏ/2, we get ℏ²/4 ≤ ‖f‖²·‖g‖². It is a direct corollary of heisenberg_bound, serving as the named reference point for [X,P] = iℏ. The `0 < hbar` hypothesis ensures we are working with a genuine physical constant rather than the trivial ℏ = 0 case.

title: Square-Root Form: From Squared to Product Inequality
content: The most familiar form of the uncertainty principle is σ_x·σ_p ≥ ℏ/2 (product of standard deviations). Going from the squared inequality ℏ²/4 ≤ ‖f‖²·‖g‖² to the product form |c|/2 ≤ ‖f‖·‖g‖ requires nonlinear arithmetic. The proof uses `nlinarith` with the witnesses `sq_abs c`, `sq_nonneg (‖f‖·‖g‖ − |c|/2)`, and a matrix inequality lemma to handle the product-of-norms structure. This pattern — introducing squared witnesses to help `nlinarith` bridge a square root — is standard for Hilbert space inequalities.
